records.source: Αὐτὸς δὲ ἐγὼ Παῦλος παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς διὰ τῆς πραΰτητος καὶ ἐπιεικείας τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὃς κατὰ πρόσωπον μὲν ταπεινὸς ἐν ὑμῖν, ἀπὼν δὲ θαρρῶ εἰς ὑμᾶς·
records.gloss: Myself but I Paul appeal to you through the meekness and gentleness of the Christ, who according to face indeed [am] humble among you, being absent but am bold toward you;
pieces: I, Paul, make this appeal to you myself, by the meekness and gentleness of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. I am the one who is humble when I am with you in person, but bold with you when I am at a distance.

L.1: Now I myself, Paul, appeal to you by the meekness and gentleness of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, I who [am] humble when face to face among you, but when absent am bold toward you.

R.1: I, Paul, am asking you this myself, and I ask it in the gentle, humble way that {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} showed. Some people say that I am humble and weak when I am with you, but bold toward you when I am far away.

decisions.choice: chapters 10-13 form a distinct section of the letter, sharp in tone: Paul's defense of his work against rivals in Corinth
alternatives: a continuation in the same tone as chapters 1-9
decisions.reason: With this verse the tone of the letter changes sharply. After the warm confidence of chapter 7 (7:4, 16) and the appeal for the collection in chapters 8-9, Paul writes with irony, warning and self-defense to the end of chapter 13. The change is widely noticed, and some have taken chapters 10-13 to be part of another letter of Paul's to Corinth, later joined to chapters 1-9. Every manuscript of 2 Corinthians has these chapters here, after chapter 9, and the translation reads them where they stand.

decisions.choice: Paul speaks emphatically in his own name
decisions.reason: Αὐτὸς δὲ ἐγὼ Παῦλος ("I myself, Paul") is unusually emphatic. The letter came from Paul and Timothy (1:1) and often says "we", but the charges answered in these chapters are against Paul himself, and he answers them in person.

decisions.choice: the meekness and gentleness of Christ: his gentle, unassuming way and his kind forbearance, the ground and manner of Paul's appeal
alternatives: Paul's own meekness, as a follower of Christ
decisions.reason: πραΰτητος is gentleness that does not assert itself; ἐπιεικείας is kindness that does not insist on its rights. Jesus called himself gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29), using words from the same roots as πραΰτητος and ταπεινὸς. Paul appeals by Christ's character, and he will act toward the Corinthians in the same way if he can.

decisions.choice: appeal: to urge earnestly
decisions.reason: παρακαλῶ is the verb used for comfort in chapters 1 and 7 (1:4; 7:6), but here, with a request following in verse 2, it has its other common sense: to urge or plead with someone (as in 2:8; 5:20).

decisions.choice: who: Paul, not Christ; the words echo what his critics say of him
alternatives: a straightforward description Paul gives of himself
decisions.reason: ὃς goes back to "I myself, Paul", not to Christ. ταπεινὸς here has the bad sense of lowly or feeble, and κατὰ πρόσωπον means "in person". Verse 10 shows that some in Corinth said Paul was forceful in his letters but weak in person; Paul repeats the charge in order to answer it. Whether these are his critics' very words is uncertain. The irony is that the lowliness they despise belongs to Christ's own way (m3).

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. The Greek has the article, and Literal keeps it.

decisions.choice: Some people say that I am humble and weak ...
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that Paul is repeating what his critics say (m5, and verse 10), and adds "weak" to show that "humble" is meant as an insult here.

records.heading: Paul defends his authority

records.source: δέομαι δὲ τὸ μὴ παρὼν θαρρῆσαι τῇ πεποιθήσει ᾗ λογίζομαι τολμῆσαι ἐπί τινας τοὺς λογιζομένους ἡμᾶς ὡς κατὰ σάρκα περιπατοῦντας.
records.gloss: I beg but the not being present to be bold with the confidence with which I reckon to be daring against some, the [ones] reckoning us as according to flesh walking.
pieces: I beg you not to make me show boldness when I am with you, the confidence that I count on using against some people, those who count us as living by merely human standards.

L.2: I beg [you] that when I am present I may not [have to] be bold with the confidence with which I reckon to be daring against some who reckon us as walking according to [the] flesh.

R.2: Please do not make me be bold and harsh with you when I come. I expect that I will have to stand up boldly to some people there. They think that we live the way selfish people do.

decisions.choice: Paul begs the church not to make it necessary for him to be severe when he comes
decisions.reason: δέομαι is a strong word for asking, "I beg". τὸ μὴ παρὼν θαρρῆσαι means "that I may not, when present, be bold": he asks the Corinthians to put things right before he arrives, so that he need not use against them the boldness his critics say he has only in letters (verse 1). He is ready to use it against "some" (13:2, 10).

decisions.choice: reckon: to count on, and to count someone as something; Paul plays on the word
decisions.reason: The same verb comes twice: λογίζομαι ("I reckon, I count on") and λογιζομένους ("those who reckon, count us"). Paul counts on being bold against those who count him as a merely human operator. The verb comes back in verses 7 and 11. τολμῆσαι ("to dare, to be daring") returns in verse 12 and 11:21.

decisions.choice: walking according to the flesh: living by merely human standards and motives
alternatives: living in a body, as a weak human being
decisions.reason: "Walk" is a Jewish way of saying "live, conduct oneself". κατὰ σάρκα ("according to the flesh") is the charge Paul answered in 1:17: that he plans and acts as people do without God, out of self-interest. Verse 3 answers it.

decisions.choice: "us": Paul himself, perhaps with his companions
alternatives: Paul and all his fellow workers equally
decisions.reason: Paul moves from "I" to "us" within the sentence. As elsewhere in the letter (1:8), the plural mostly means Paul, since the charge is against him (verses 1, 10).

decisions.choice: living by merely human standards (B); live the way selfish people do (R)
decisions.reason: As in 1:17 and 5:16, Literal keeps "flesh", while Balanced and Readable give the sense (m3). "Worldly" is avoided because it would blur the word with "world".

decisions.choice: count on ... count us
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps Paul's play on the one verb (m2) with an everyday English word.

records.source: ἐν σαρκὶ γὰρ περιπατοῦντες οὐ κατὰ σάρκα στρατευόμεθα τὰ γὰρ ὅπλα τῆς στρατείας ἡμῶν οὐ σαρκικὰ ἀλλὰ δυνατὰ τῷ θεῷ πρὸς καθαίρεσιν ὀχυρωμάτων λογισμοὺς καθαιροῦντες καὶ πᾶν ὕψωμα ἐπαιρόμενον κατὰ τῆς γνώσεως τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ αἰχμαλωτίζοντες πᾶν νόημα εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ ἐν ἑτοίμῳ ἔχοντες ἐκδικῆσαι πᾶσαν παρακοήν, ὅταν πληρωθῇ ὑμῶν ἡ ὑπακοή.
records.gloss: In flesh for walking not according to flesh do we wage war, \v 4 for the weapons of the warfare of us [are] not fleshly but powerful to the God for demolition of strongholds, arguments demolishing \v 5 and every high thing lifting itself up against the knowledge of the God, and taking captive every thought into the obedience of the Christ, \v 6 and in readiness having to punish every disobedience, whenever may be fulfilled of you the obedience.
pieces: We do live as human beings, but we do not fight our battles by merely human standards.
Our weapons in this fight are not merely human; they have power from God to tear down strongholds, and so we tear down arguments
and every proud tower raised against the knowledge of God. We capture every thought and lead it away to obey {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
We are prepared to punish all disobedience, once you yourselves have fully obeyed.

L.3: For though walking in [the] flesh, we do not wage war according to [the] flesh,
L.4: for the weapons of our warfare [are] not fleshly but powerful to God for [the] tearing down of strongholds, [as we are] tearing down arguments
L.5: and every high thing lifting itself up against the knowledge of God, and taking captive every thought into the obedience of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}},
L.6: and holding ourselves in readiness to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is made full.

R.3: We are human, but we do not fight our battles the way humans usually do.
R.4: Our weapons are not human weapons. They have God's power, and they can knock down strong forts. We knock down clever arguments
R.5: and every proud wall that people build to keep themselves from knowing God. We capture every thought, like a prisoner of war, and make it obey {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
R.6: And once you have fully obeyed, we are ready to punish anyone who still disobeys.

decisions.choice: in the flesh: in ordinary, weak human life; according to the flesh, fleshly: by merely human standards and means
alternatives: both phrases in the same, bad sense
decisions.reason: Paul answers the charge of verse 2 with a play on words. ἐν σαρκὶ ("in flesh") is simply being human, as in Galatians 2:20; κατὰ σάρκα ("according to flesh") and σαρκικὰ ("fleshly") mean working by human standards, without God. He is human, but his methods are not merely human.

decisions.choice: a picture of siege warfare: fortresses torn down, towers brought low, prisoners led away
decisions.reason: στρατευόμεθα means to serve as a soldier or wage a campaign. ὀχυρωμάτων were fortresses; ὕψωμα is anything raised high, such as a tower or rampart; αἰχμαλωτίζοντες means to take prisoner in war. The picture is of an army that pulls down a city's defenses and leads its people away captive. Paul uses the same kind of picture for God's weapons in 6:7 and Ephesians 6:11-17.

decisions.choice: tearing down strongholds may echo Proverbs 21:22
decisions.reason: The Greek of Proverbs 21:22 uses the same noun, ὀχύρωμα, for the stronghold of the ungodly that a wise man pulls down. In Paul's picture the strongholds are arguments and proud thoughts (verse 5), not places.

decisions.choice: powerful to God: made powerful by God, mighty in his service
decisions.reason: The dative τῷ θεῷ can mean "by God" (the power comes from him), "for God" (in his cause), or, as a Hebrew-style intensive, "mighty before God", that is, very mighty (compare the Greek of Jonah 3:3, "a city great to God"). In each reading the weapons' power is not human; "by God" fits the contrast with "fleshly" best.

decisions.choice: arguments: reasoned objections; every high thing: every proud barrier against knowing God
decisions.reason: λογισμοὺς are reasonings, calculations or arguments: here the clever case made against Paul and his gospel, and the kind of reasoning prized in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:19-20; 3:20). "The knowledge of God" is knowing God, which the gospel brings (2:14; 4:6); every proud argument raised against it is a tower to be brought down.

decisions.choice: every thought taken captive into obedience to Christ
alternatives: every thought of Paul's own only
decisions.reason: νόημα is a thought, plan or scheme (2:11; 4:4; 11:3). τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ is the obedience owed to Christ: the captured thoughts are made to serve him. The picture continues the war: prisoners led away under a new master.

decisions.choice: Paul will punish the disobedience of those who still resist, once the church as a whole has returned to obedience
alternatives: the Corinthians' own disobedience in general
decisions.reason: ἐκδικῆσαι means to punish or see justice done, not personal revenge. "Your obedience" is the church's (2:9; 7:15); "every disobedience" is then what remains among those who still oppose Paul (13:2). The participles of verses 4-6 are loosely joined to "we wage war" in verse 3, as Paul's long sentences often are.

decisions.choice: live as human beings ... by merely human standards ... not merely human (B); human ... the way humans usually do ... not human weapons (R)
alternatives: in the flesh ... according to the flesh ... fleshly
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "flesh" so the wordplay can be traced; Balanced and Readable give the sense of each phrase (m1), as in verse 2.

decisions.choice: tearing down ... tearing down (L); tear down ... tear down (B); knock down ... knock down (R)
decisions.reason: The noun and the participle come from one verb, which returns in verse 8 ("not for tearing you down"); each level keeps one English verb for all three.

decisions.choice: every proud wall that people build to keep themselves from knowing God; like a prisoner of war; anyone who still disobeys
alternatives: every high thing raised against the knowledge of God
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the picture and says whose disobedience is punished (m5, m6, m7).

decisions.choice: the long sentence broken into four (B) or six (R)
decisions.reason: Verses 3-6 are one Greek sentence; Balanced and Readable break it where each clause can stand, keeping its order. Readable puts the time clause of verse 6 first.

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. The Greek has the article, and Literal keeps it.

records.gloss: The [things] according to face you look at.
pieces: Look at what is right in front of you.

L.7: Look at the things before [your] face.

R.7: Look at the facts that are right in front of your eyes.

decisions.choice: a command: look at what is plain to see
alternatives: a statement: you look at things only as they appear on the outside
a question: are you looking at outward appearances?
decisions.reason: βλέπετε can be read as a command or as a statement, since the forms are the same; the SBLGNT ends the sentence with a full stop, not a question mark, though a question is grammatically possible. Paul often uses this verb as a command (1 Corinthians 8:9; 10:12; 16:10; Philippians 3:2), and the next sentence goes on to point out a plain fact: Paul belongs to Christ as much as anyone. Read as a statement, the words are a rebuke: the Corinthians judge by outward show, as in 5:12 and 10:10. Both readings fit the passage.

decisions.choice: the things before your face: what is evident, in plain view
alternatives: outward appearances, as against what is within
decisions.reason: κατὰ πρόσωπον is the phrase of verse 1, "face to face". As a command, it points to facts the Corinthians can see for themselves, such as Paul's work among them (3:2-3). As a statement, it would mean appearances, as "in the face" does in 5:12.

decisions.choice: the facts
decisions.reason: Readable names what is in plain view (m2).

records.source: εἴ τις πέποιθεν ἑαυτῷ Χριστοῦ εἶναι, τοῦτο λογιζέσθω πάλιν ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ὅτι καθὼς αὐτὸς Χριστοῦ οὕτως καὶ ἡμεῖς.
records.gloss: If anyone is confident in himself of Christ to be, this let him reckon again within himself, that just as he [is] of Christ, so also we.
pieces: Anyone who is confident of belonging to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} should think again and consider this: just as that person belongs to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, so do we.

L.7: If anyone is confident in {{gender:themselves|himself}} that {{gender:they are|he is}} of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, let {{gender:them|him}} reckon this again within {{gender:themselves|himself}}: that just as {{gender:they are|he is}} of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, so also [are] we.

R.7: Some people are sure that they belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. They should stop and think again. If they belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, then so do we.

decisions.choice: to be of Christ: to belong to Christ, as his servant
alternatives: to belong to a party that claims Christ's name (1 Corinthians 1:12)
decisions.reason: Χριστοῦ εἶναι ("to be of Christ") means belonging to him. Paul's rivals claimed a special standing as Christ's servants (11:23). The words recall the slogan "I am of Christ" in 1 Corinthians 1:12, but nothing here shows that the same group is meant.

decisions.choice: Paul does not deny the claim but sets his own beside it
decisions.reason: λογιζέσθω is the verb "reckon" of verse 2, now as a command in the third person: let such a person count again. Paul grants for the moment that his rival belongs to Christ and asks only that the same be granted to him. Later he goes further (11:13-15).

decisions.choice: {{gender:themselves|himself}}; {{gender:they are|he is}}; {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: τις ("anyone") is general, so the default pronouns are inclusive. Balanced says "that person" and Readable uses the plural, which need no setting.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

records.source: ἐάν τε γὰρ περισσότερόν τι καυχήσωμαι περὶ τῆς ἐξουσίας ἡμῶν, ἧς ἔδωκεν ὁ κύριος εἰς οἰκοδομὴν καὶ οὐκ εἰς καθαίρεσιν ὑμῶν, οὐκ αἰσχυνθήσομαι, ἵνα μὴ δόξω ὡς ἂν ἐκφοβεῖν ὑμᾶς διὰ τῶν ἐπιστολῶν·
records.gloss: If even for more abundantly something I should boast about the authority of us, which gave the Lord for building up and not for tearing down of you, not I will be put to shame, \v 9 so that not I may seem as if to frighten you through the letters;
pieces: Suppose I boast rather more than I should about our authority, which the Lord gave us to build you up and not to tear you down: I will not be put to shame.
I would not want it to look as though I were out to terrify you by letter.

L.8: For even if I boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave for building [you] up and not for tearing you down, I will not be put to shame,
L.9: so that I may not seem as though [I were] frightening you through [my] letters.

R.8: Even if I boast a bit too much about the authority we have from the Lord, that boasting will not put me to shame. The Lord gave us this authority to build you up, not to knock you down.
R.9: I do not want you to think I am just trying to scare you with my letters.

decisions.choice: to boast: to speak with pride of one's standing; here Paul begins the boasting his rivals have forced on him
alternatives: proper pride in God's work only
decisions.reason: καυχήσωμαι begins the run of words for boasting that carries chapters 10-12 (10:13-17; 11:16-18, 30; 12:1, 5-6, 9). Paul's rivals boast of themselves; Paul is drawn into boasting too, but he boasts of the authority the Lord gave him and, later, of his weaknesses (11:30; 12:9). περισσότερόν τι ("somewhat more") grants that it may seem excessive.

decisions.choice: authority: the right and power of an apostle, given by the Lord for building the church up
decisions.reason: ἐξουσίας is the authority of an apostle, given by "the Lord", here Christ, who sent him (1:1). Paul says the same in nearly the same words in 13:10. καθαίρεσιν picks up the "tearing down" of strongholds in verse 4: Paul's power tears down proud arguments, but it was given to build up the church, not to tear it down.

decisions.choice: building up and tearing down: the words of Jeremiah's call
decisions.reason: God appointed Jeremiah to tear down and to build (Jeremiah 1:10; 24:6). Paul describes his own commission in the same terms, with the stress on building.

decisions.choice: I will not be put to shame: his boast will prove true; and so his letters are not empty threats
alternatives: "so that" goes with an unspoken "I say this"
decisions.reason: αἰσχυνθήσομαι means his boast will not be shown up as empty. Verse 9 begins with ἵνα ("so that"), with no main verb close at hand. It may go with "I will not be put to shame": what he does will match what he writes, so his letters will not seem a mere attempt to frighten. Or Paul may leave unspoken "I say this", as in 1 Corinthians 7:6. The sense is much the same.

decisions.choice: boast
decisions.reason: Elsewhere Balanced and Readable often speak of pride, but in chapters 10-12 Paul's argument turns on the word "boast" itself, ironically used, so every level keeps it, as in 1 Corinthians 1:29-31 (the settled choice on boasting).

decisions.choice: The Lord gave us this authority to build you up, not to knock you down.
alternatives: which the Lord gave for building up and not for tearing down
decisions.reason: Readable makes the relative clause a sentence of its own, naming the Lord again. "Knock down" repeats the verb of verse 4 at this level.

records.source: ὅτι Αἱ ἐπιστολαὶ μέν, φησίν, βαρεῖαι καὶ ἰσχυραί, ἡ δὲ παρουσία τοῦ σώματος ἀσθενὴς καὶ ὁ λόγος ἐξουθενημένος.
records.gloss: Because the letters indeed, he says, [are] weighty and strong, but the presence of the body weak and the speech having been despised.
pieces: For someone says, "His letters are weighty and strong, but when he is here in person he is weak, and the way he speaks is contemptible."

L.10: For "[His] letters," he says, "[are] weighty and strong, but the presence of [his] body [is] weak and [his] speech despised."

R.10: Someone there says, "His letters are strong and hard-hitting. But when he is with us in person, he is weak, and his speaking is not worth listening to."

decisions.choice: the words after "for" quote what a critic says about Paul
decisions.reason: Ancient manuscripts have no quotation marks, but φησίν ("he says") marks the words around it as speech, and the SBLGNT begins them with a capital letter. The quotation runs to the end of the verse.

decisions.choice: he says: a particular critic, or "someone says"
decisions.reason: φησίν is singular. It may point to one leading critic, whom verse 11 calls "such a person", or it may be used loosely for what is being said. The opponents in chapters 10-12 are spoken of both as "some" (verses 2, 12) and as "anyone" (verse 7; 11:4).

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "he says" (singular)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have the plural, "they say", which differs by one letter and matches the plurals of verses 2 and 12. The SBLGNT reads the singular, found in most manuscripts. The meaning is close either way. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: weighty and strong letters; feeble presence in person; speaking held in contempt
decisions.reason: βαρεῖαι means heavy, so weighty, impressive or severe; ἰσχυραί means strong, forceful. παρουσία τοῦ σώματος is Paul's presence in person, and ἐξουθενημένος means despised, treated as nothing. In Corinth eloquent speech and an impressive bearing were admired; Paul admits he was untrained in speech (11:6) and had not come with fine words (1 Corinthians 2:1-4).

decisions.choice: when he is here in person (B); when he is with us in person (R)
decisions.reason: "Presence of the body" means how he comes across in person (m4); Balanced and Readable say so.

decisions.choice: someone says (B); Someone there says (R)
decisions.reason: "Someone" leaves open whether one critic is meant (m2). Readable puts the speaker first, as English usually does.

records.source: τοῦτο λογιζέσθω ὁ τοιοῦτος, ὅτι οἷοί ἐσμεν τῷ λόγῳ δι’ ἐπιστολῶν ἀπόντες, τοιοῦτοι καὶ παρόντες τῷ ἔργῳ.
records.gloss: This let reckon such a one, that such as we are in word through letters being absent, such also being present in deed.
pieces: Anyone who says this should understand that we are the same in action when we are with you as we are in the words of our letters when we are away.

L.11: Let such a person reckon this: that what we are in word through letters when absent, such [we are] also in deed when present.

R.11: People who talk like that should know this: when we come, what we do will be just as strong as what we write in our letters when we are away.

decisions.choice: such a person: whoever says what verse 10 quotes
decisions.reason: ὁ τοιοῦτος points back to the speaker of verse 10, without naming him. λογιζέσθω ("let him reckon") is the verb of verses 2 and 7 again: let the critics count on this.

decisions.choice: Paul is the same in word and in deed, and his next visit will show it
decisions.reason: οἷοί ... τοιοῦτοι ("such as ... such") sets the two halves side by side; the verb of the second half is understood. The present tense states what Paul always is, but the point is the visit to come (12:20-13:2, 10).

decisions.choice: when we come, what we do will be just as strong
alternatives: such we are also in deed when present
decisions.reason: Readable says what the sentence means for the coming visit (m2).

records.source: Οὐ γὰρ τολμῶμεν ἐγκρῖναι ἢ συγκρῖναι ἑαυτούς τισιν τῶν ἑαυτοὺς συνιστανόντων· ἀλλὰ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἑαυτοὺς μετροῦντες καὶ συγκρίνοντες ἑαυτοὺς ἑαυτοῖς οὐ συνιᾶσιν.
records.gloss: Not for we dare to class or to compare ourselves with some of the [ones] themselves commending; but they, by themselves themselves measuring and comparing themselves with themselves, not do understand.
pieces: We would not dare to put ourselves in the same class as some of those who recommend themselves, or to set ourselves beside them. They use themselves as the measuring stick and compare themselves with themselves, and that shows how little they understand.

L.12: For we do not dare to class or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves; but they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, do not understand.

R.12: We would never dare to put ourselves in the same group as those people who recommend themselves, or even to compare ourselves with them. They make up their own standards, and then they measure themselves by those standards. They compare themselves with each other. They do not understand anything!

decisions.choice: we do not dare: ironic; Paul will not stoop to the rivals' kind of comparison
decisions.reason: τολμῶμεν ("we dare") picks up the daring of verse 2, and Paul says it with irony: these people are so impressive that he would not dare join their ranks. ἐγκρῖναι and συγκρῖναι sound alike, "to class with" and "to compare with", a play on words.

decisions.choice: those who recommend themselves
decisions.reason: συνιστανόντων is the verb of 3:1; 4:2; 5:12, used for introducing and vouching for someone, as letters of recommendation did. The rivals recommend themselves; verse 18 says whose recommendation counts.

decisions.choice: they measure themselves by their own standard
alternatives: they measure themselves by one another, within their own group
decisions.reason: ἑαυτοῖς ἑαυτοὺς can mean each measures himself by himself, or they measure themselves among themselves. Either way there is no standard outside themselves, and no measure from God, which is what verses 13-16 go on to speak of.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "they do not understand", with "but we" at the start of verse 13
alternatives: the words are lacking, so that the measuring by oneself in verse 12 describes Paul
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts, mostly Greek-Latin ones, lack οὐ συνιᾶσιν and the opening words of verse 13, which turns the sentence around: Paul and his companions measure themselves by themselves and do not boast beyond measure. The SBLGNT follows the longer text, found in most manuscripts, including early ones. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: recommend
decisions.reason: As in 3:1 and 5:12, Balanced says "recommend", which keeps the link with letters of recommendation (m2); Readable does the same here so that verse 18 can repeat it. Literal says "commend".

decisions.choice: put ourselves in the same class as ... set ourselves beside them
decisions.reason: Balanced gives each of the two similar verbs its own phrase (m1).

decisions.choice: They make up their own standards
decisions.reason: Readable says what measuring oneself by oneself means (m3).

records.heading: Boasting within the measure God gives

records.source: ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐκ εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα καυχησόμεθα, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τοῦ κανόνος οὗ ἐμέρισεν ἡμῖν ὁ θεὸς μέτρου, ἐφικέσθαι ἄχρι καὶ ὑμῶν οὐ γὰρ ὡς μὴ ἐφικνούμενοι εἰς ὑμᾶς ὑπερεκτείνομεν ἑαυτούς, ἄχρι γὰρ καὶ ὑμῶν ἐφθάσαμεν ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ τοῦ Χριστοῦ οὐκ εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα καυχώμενοι ἐν ἀλλοτρίοις κόποις, ἐλπίδα δὲ ἔχοντες αὐξανομένης τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν ἐν ὑμῖν μεγαλυνθῆναι κατὰ τὸν κανόνα ἡμῶν εἰς περισσείαν, εἰς τὰ ὑπερέκεινα ὑμῶν εὐαγγελίσασθαι, οὐκ ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ κανόνι εἰς τὰ ἕτοιμα καυχήσασθαι.
records.gloss: We but not into the [things] beyond measure will boast, but according to the measure of the sphere which apportioned to us the God, of a measure, to reach as far as even you. \v 14 Not for as not reaching to you are we overextending ourselves, as far as for even you we came in the gospel of the Christ, \v 15 not into the [things] beyond measure boasting in others' labors, hope but having, increasing the faith of you, among you to be enlarged according to the sphere of us into abundance, \v 16 into the [places] beyond you to proclaim the gospel, not in another's sphere into the [things] ready to boast.
pieces: But we will not boast of things outside our measure. We will boast only within the measure of the field that God has measured out to us as ours, and it reaches even as far as you.
We are not overstretching ourselves, as we would be if our field did not reach you; we did reach you, bringing the gospel of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
We do not boast of things outside our measure, in work that others have done. We hope instead that as your faith grows, we will be given far more room among you, still within our field,
so that we can carry the gospel to the lands beyond you, without boasting of ground someone else has already prepared.

L.13: But we will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the sphere which God apportioned to us as a measure, to reach even as far as you.
L.14: For we are not overextending ourselves, as [though we] did not reach to you, for we came even as far as you in the gospel of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}},
L.15: not boasting beyond measure in the labors of others, but having hope that, as your faith grows, we will be enlarged among you according to our sphere, to overflowing,
L.16: so as to proclaim the gospel in the [lands] beyond you, not to boast in another's sphere of things [already] made ready.

R.13: But we will not boast about things outside the limits God set for us. We will boast only about the work in the area God gave us, and that area reaches all the way to you.
R.14: We are not stretching the truth when we boast about you. We really did come all the way to you; we were the first to bring you the good news about {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
R.15: We do not boast about work that other people have done. We hope that your faith will keep growing. Then our work among you can become much bigger, but still in the area God gave us.
R.16: Then we can tell the good news in places far beyond you. We do not want to boast about what someone else has already done in their own area.

decisions.choice: an assigned field of work, measured out to Paul by God
alternatives: a rule or standard of conduct
a limit set on Paul's boasting
decisions.reason: κανών first meant a measuring rod, then a rule or standard (Galatians 6:16), and also a measured-out area. Here it is something that "reaches as far as you", that has room to grow "beyond you", and that can belong to someone else (verse 16), so a field of work is meant. Paul's field was the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7-9), and his practice was to preach where Christ was not yet known, not to build on another's foundation (Romans 15:20).

decisions.choice: beyond measure, measure: Paul's boasting stays within what God measured out
decisions.reason: Paul piles up the language of measuring: μέτρον and μέτρου ("measure"), ἄμετρα twice ("things without measure", verses 13 and 15), and the "sphere" three times. It answers verse 12, where the rivals measure themselves by themselves. Paul's measure is set by God, and Corinth lies inside it.

decisions.choice: we came: we reached you, and were in fact the first to bring you the gospel
alternatives: we came first (the verb itself stressing priority)
decisions.reason: ἐφθάσαμεν can mean "come first, precede" or simply "arrive, reach". Either way it is a fact that Paul founded the church in Corinth (Acts 18:1-11; 1 Corinthians 3:6, 10; 4:15); the rivals came later.

decisions.choice: boasting in other people's labors: taking credit for work others did
decisions.reason: Paul does not boast of churches others founded, and by implication his rivals do, having come into a church he founded. ἕτοιμα ("things made ready") is ground already prepared by someone else.

decisions.choice: as the Corinthians' faith grows, Paul's work will be enlarged through them and reach further
alternatives: Paul will be greatly praised among them
decisions.reason: μεγαλυνθῆναι means to be made larger, or to be praised. The words that follow, "according to our sphere" and "so as to preach beyond you", favor the first: once the Corinthians' faith is strong, Paul's work, based among them, can grow and go on to new places. ἐν ὑμῖν may mean "among you" or "by you".

decisions.choice: the lands beyond you: places further west not yet reached with the gospel
decisions.reason: Paul does not name them. In Romans 15:23-24, 28 he speaks of plans to go to Spain by way of Rome.

decisions.choice: your faith: the Corinthians' trust in Christ
decisions.reason: πίστεως is their faith, growing and becoming steady, so that they no longer need Paul's constant attention.

decisions.choice: boast
decisions.reason: As in verse 8, every level keeps "boast", on which the argument of chapters 10-12 turns.

decisions.choice: sphere (L); field (B); area (R)
decisions.reason: Each level keeps one word for all three uses, so that "another's" field in verse 16 is plainly the same kind of thing as Paul's. Balanced says "field", which can mean both an area and a line of work.

decisions.choice: the long sentence broken into five (B) or nine (R)
decisions.reason: Verses 13-16 are one Greek sentence; Balanced and Readable break it where each clause can stand.

decisions.choice: We are not stretching the truth when we boast about you. ... we were the first to bring you
decisions.reason: Readable says what overreaching means here, and states the fact behind the verb (m3).

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. The Greek has the article, and Literal keeps it.

records.source: Ὁ δὲ καυχώμενος ἐν κυρίῳ καυχάσθω·
records.gloss: The [one] but boasting in [the] Lord let him boast;
pieces: But, as Scripture says, "Whoever boasts should boast in the Lord."

L.17: But "The one who boasts must boast in [the] Lord."

R.17: But, as Scripture says, "Anyone who wants to boast should boast only about the Lord."

decisions.choice: a shortened quotation of Jeremiah 9:23-24 (9:22-23 in the Hebrew numbering), the line Paul also quotes in 1 Corinthians 1:31
decisions.reason: Jeremiah 9:23-24 tells the wise, the strong and the rich not to boast of what they have, but to boast that they understand and know God. Paul quotes the same line in 1 Corinthians 1:31, there with "as it is written"; here he gives it without a formula, as a principle that settles the question of verses 12-16. The Greek of 1 Samuel 2:10 has similar words.

decisions.choice: the Lord: in Jeremiah, God's own name; here most likely Christ
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew of Jeremiah 9:24 the word is the divine name, YHWH. Paul quotes it with κυρίῳ ("Lord"). In verse 8 "the Lord" gave Paul his authority, and for Paul "the Lord" is usually Christ, so here too the Lord is most likely Christ, as in 1 Corinthians 1:31.

decisions.choice: but: the right kind of boasting, set against the rivals'
decisions.reason: δὲ turns from boasting in other people's work (verses 15-16) to the boasting Scripture allows: in what the Lord has done (compare Romans 15:17-18).

decisions.choice: Lord
decisions.reason: The style guide keeps "the LORD" for the divine name in the Old Testament itself. Here Paul quotes the verse with the Greek word for "Lord", as John 1:23 does; meaning decision m2 explains whom it means.

decisions.choice: The one who boasts must boast (L); Whoever boasts should boast (B); Anyone who wants to boast should boast only (R)
decisions.reason: The same words as 1 Corinthians 1:31 at each level, so the reader can see that it is the same quotation. The Greek is a command in the third person; English uses "must" or "should" and avoids a masculine pronoun for a saying that applies to anyone.

decisions.choice: as Scripture says
decisions.reason: Paul gives no formula here, but the line is a quotation (m1); Balanced and Readable say so, as they do in 1 Corinthians 1:31.

records.source: οὐ γὰρ ὁ ἑαυτὸν συνιστάνων, ἐκεῖνός ἐστιν δόκιμος, ἀλλὰ ὃν ὁ κύριος συνίστησιν.
records.gloss: Not for the [one] himself commending, that one is approved, but whom the Lord commends.
pieces: The person who stands approved is not the one who recommends {{gender:themselves|himself}}, but the one the Lord recommends.

L.18: For the one approved is not the one who commends {{gender:themselves|himself}}, but [the one] whom the Lord commends.

R.18: People who recommend themselves are not the ones who are truly approved. The ones who are approved are those the Lord recommends.

decisions.choice: approved: tested and found genuine
decisions.reason: δόκιμος was used of coins or metal tested and found true. Paul uses words from the same root in 2:9 and 8:2, and in 13:5-7 he will ask the Corinthians to test themselves, since they wanted proof of him.

decisions.choice: to recommend: to vouch for someone; the only recommendation that counts is the Lord's
decisions.reason: συνιστάνων and συνίστησιν are the verb of verse 12 and of 3:1; 5:12. The rivals recommend themselves; Paul's recommendation comes from the Lord, and the church in Corinth is itself his letter of recommendation (3:2-3).

decisions.choice: the Lord: Christ, as in verses 8 and 17
decisions.reason: κύριος continues the quotation in verse 17, where the Lord is most likely Christ.

decisions.choice: that one: an emphatic pointer back to the self-recommender
decisions.reason: ἐκεῖνός picks up "the one who recommends himself" with emphasis: that person is not the approved one.

decisions.choice: commends (L); recommends (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 12: Literal says "commend", Balanced and Readable "recommend".

decisions.choice: {{gender:themselves|himself}}
decisions.reason: The saying applies to anyone, so the default is inclusive. Readable uses the plural, which needs no setting.

decisions.choice: the approved one named first (L, B); two sentences (R)
alternatives: not the one commending himself, that one is approved
decisions.reason: The Greek order (m4) does not work in English; the levels state the contrast in a clear order.
